network:
New to Reticulum? Start here →

Everyday use shaped the links and software behind ciXnet.

Making access familiar

NomadNet gave our early network a purpose beyond messaging. Its text-based interface appealed to us as engineers and enthusiasts, but getting our users comfortable with it was harder.

We wanted people to use the network every day. Looking something up or checking a page needed to become ordinary. If every visit felt like a technical excursion or a resilience exercise, people would return to their usual tools.

That shaped NomadPL and our clients. Most of our users now access the NomadPL network in Chrome through our browser bridge. Compression helps keep the pages small, and in our use the additional latency has been minimal.

Moving the backbone to HaLow

As use increased, LoRa links between nodes became a bottleneck. A few users active together could fill the available airtime, causing traffic to back up and connections to become choppy.

Wi-Fi HaLow removed that bottleneck in our installations, with comparable—and on some links better—range. We still use LoRa for inexpensive last-mile connections.

hardware:
LoRa nodes for phones and laptops

Small LoRa nodes with Bluetooth give phones and laptops a convenient way onto the network. We use them for last-mile connections where their low cost and reach make them useful.

We started installing more nodes permanently, including wiring them into vehicles. Having a node already fitted and powered removes the need to find it, charge it and connect everything before each use.

The less our users have to handle the network equipment, the more often they use the network. A node in the car becomes part of the car rather than another piece of equipment to remember.

Installation reports

Read about the way we use these components and the choices behind our installations.

Permanent vehicle nodes →HaLow backbone links →

Putting the components together

The charge controller and battery supply power. HaLow connects to the Raspberry Pi through Ethernet; the LoRa node connects to the Pi through USB. The cooler provides an inexpensive enclosure for the assembly.

assistance:
Depending on the scope of your project and our availability, we may be able to assist with network planning, rollout and engineering.

Enquire to discuss your requirements and possible arrangements.

Site assessments

An assessment establishes what is available at a location and what will be needed for an installation. This can include existing communications equipment, mounting positions, power supplies, cable routes and access for installation and maintenance.

For an existing network, the work may involve reviewing the current arrangement, investigating problem areas and identifying changes needed for an extension or upgrade. The findings provide a basis for equipment selection, installation work and cost planning.

Terrain & coverage surveys

Terrain, vegetation, buildings and antenna height affect the links a network can support. Survey work can examine elevation profiles, potential obstructions and candidate locations to help determine where equipment should be placed.

Depending on the project, this may involve map-based analysis, visits to proposed sites and practical link tests. The results can inform antenna positions, intermediate node locations and the choice of radio equipment. Areas requiring further measurements can be identified before deployment.

Network design & deployment planning

Network design brings together the locations to be served, expected traffic, available links and the services users need. The work can cover topology, backbone and access links, equipment specifications, power requirements and integration with existing infrastructure.

Deployment planning sets out how that design will be put into service. This may include a pilot installation, staged expansion, equipment preparation, installation schedules and commissioning procedures. Configuration records and maintenance requirements can be included so the deployed system can be managed consistently.

Software engineering

We may be able to undertake application development, service integration and adaptations for project-specific requirements. This can include Reticulum-based applications, interfaces to existing systems, configuration tools and software used to operate the network.

The work begins with the required behaviour and the systems involved. From there, the scope can define the implementation, testing, documentation and arrangements for ongoing maintenance. Existing ciXnet components may form part of a solution where they suit the requirements.

Implementation & commissioning

Implementation assistance can cover equipment configuration, node preparation, installation support and bringing services into operation. For deployments across several locations, repeatable configurations and clear equipment records help keep the installations consistent.

Commissioning can include checking link performance, service access and the way the system behaves under its intended workload. Handover documentation can record the installed equipment, settings, test results and procedures needed by the people responsible for it.

Project enquiries

Please include a description of the project, the locations involved and any existing equipment or infrastructure. Outline the work you would like us to undertake, along with your timeframe and budget where established.

We can then discuss the scope, possible arrangements and whether we are able to take it on.

about:
ciXnet is a group working on independent communications, with Reticulum at the centre of our network.

How we got started

Rural power outages got us looking at other ways to stay connected. The first experiments involved an antenna at home, a truck connection, a laptop and eventually a friend joining the network.

NomadNet pages made that early network useful. A computer at home could answer a page request without someone being there to respond. As more people joined, we worked on the things that made access easier and connections more useful.

Where that led

We developed NomadPL to present information in a familiar form, and the ciXnet client to bring browsing and messaging together. We moved our backbone links to HaLow as everyday traffic increased, while keeping inexpensive LoRa nodes for local access.

This site brings together the projects, configuration guides and accounts of that work.

How the network developed →Software & services →Build reports →

Development

Our published software is available on GitHub. We use OpenAI Codex for assistance with development, debugging and testing, with human review of the work.

projects/nomadpl:
NomadPL carries HTML pages, stylesheets, images and web applications over Reticulum. The ciXnet client provides a built-in browser and a browser bridge for access through a regular browser.

Python 3.11 or newer · MIT licence · Experimental release

Configuration →Downloads & releases ↗Source on GitHub ↗Support & issues ↗
Why we built itHow it fits togetherConfiguration

Why we built it

NomadNet was an important part of how we got started with Reticulum. Hosting pages gave our network a purpose beyond messaging: information could be available even when nobody was there to answer. Its text-based interface also appealed to us as engineers and enthusiasts, with something of the BTX and early online-service experience.

Getting our users on board was harder. They were accustomed to browsing websites and had little interest in an interface that felt like going back to the 1980s. With NomadNet, they were always conscious of entering a separate environment, with its own controls and conventions.

We wanted people to use the network every day. Looking something up, reading a page or checking for updates needed to become ordinary activities. If every visit felt like a technical excursion or a resilience exercise, people would try it out and then return to their usual tools.

That shaped our development of NomadPL and the ciXnet clients. NomadPL provides HTML pages and familiar navigation. The ciXnet client includes a built-in browser and a browser bridge that lets people access those pages through the browser they already use. Most of our users now browse the NomadPL network in Chrome. They can open a page and follow links without learning a separate browsing environment.

Keeping transfers small remains part of the design. Compression helps limit the overhead of the richer pages, and in our use the additional latency has been small. Making the network comfortable enough for everyday use has been as important to us as getting the underlying connections working.

How it fits together

ACCESSYour browserChrome or another browser
↔
LOCAL COMPUTERciXnet clientBrowser bridge
↔
RETICULUMNomadPL sitePages & applications

The ciXnet client provides two ways to browse: its built-in browser, or a regular browser connected through the client’s browser bridge. The client requests pages from remote NomadPL destinations over Reticulum. Existing Reticulum interfaces carry the traffic.

NomadPL sites use the nomadpl.node destination namespace. NomadNet uses nomadnetwork.node. The two can run alongside each other; each has its own destinations and discovery.

Configuration & getting started

For everyday browsing, use the ciXnet client’s built-in browser or its browser bridge. The commands below cover the standalone NomadPL package and its command-line tools.

The standalone package requires Python 3.11 or newer and Reticulum connectivity between the browsing computer and the site. Download a release or clone the repository, then run the following installation command from its source directory.

INSTALL FROM THE SOURCE DIRECTORY
python -m pip install .

Serve a site

The repository includes a small example site. This command serves it and keeps the site's identity outside the published directory.

SITE COMPUTER
nomadpl serve --root examples/site --identity state/home.identity --name "My site"

The command prints the site's nomadpl:// address. Keep the identity file: it determines the destination address.

Standalone browser testing

The standalone package also includes a command-line gateway for testing a site without the ciXnet client. On a connected browsing computer, replace DESTINATION_HASH with the destination printed by the site command.

BROWSING COMPUTER
nomadpl browse nomadpl://DESTINATION_HASH/ --port 8080

Open the local HTTP address printed by the bridge. The bridge listens on loopback, and each destination gets its own browser hostname.

projects/retdns:
retdns associates a readable name with a Reticulum destination address. Applications can look up a name, obtain the address and connect using the destination’s own protocol.

Python 3.11 or newer · MIT licence · Experimental release

Configuration →Downloads & releases ↗Source on GitHub ↗Support & issues ↗

Finding a service by name

Destination hashes identify services on Reticulum, but they are awkward to share and recognise. retdns provides a registry of names and their corresponding destination addresses, with forward and reverse lookups.

REQUESThome.cixA name entered by a user
↔
RESOLUTIONretdns registryThe selected name server
→
CONNECTIONDestinationNomadPL or another application

Each registry maintains one name for each address and one address for each name. Clients select the server whose records they want to use. The .cix suffix is used for ciXnet names; the software also accepts other domain-style names.

Discovery & caching

Name servers announce themselves under retdns.server. Discovery lets clients find available services; clients query a selected server by its destination address.

Successful lookups are stored locally until their TTL expires. The cache survives application restarts and stores both the forward and reverse mapping. Server records remain registered until changed or removed.

Configuration & getting started

Download a release or clone the repository. From its source directory, install the package in a Python 3.11 or newer environment with Reticulum connectivity.

INSTALL FROM SOURCE
python -m pip install .

Register a name

Replace APPLICATION_DESTINATION with the actual application destination hash. For a NomadPL site, use the address printed by its serve command.

SERVER COMPUTER
retdns records add home.cix APPLICATION_DESTINATION
retdns records list
retdns serve --name "Community DNS"

The server prints its own destination address. Use that address as DNS_SERVER_DESTINATION in client queries.

Look up a destination

CLIENT COMPUTER
retdns discover --seconds 15
retdns lookup home.cix --server DNS_SERVER_DESTINATION

Queries return the name, destination address and TTL. To look up the name assigned to an address, use a reverse query.

REVERSE LOOKUP
retdns reverse APPLICATION_DESTINATION --server DNS_SERVER_DESTINATION

projects/client:
The ciXnet client brings browsing, messaging and network access into one application.

Built-in browser →Browser bridge →NomadPL →Name resolution →

Built-in browsing

The client includes its own browser for accessing network pages. Users can browse within the application without opening a separate browser.

Use your regular browser

The client also provides a browser bridge. This lets users access NomadPL pages through Chrome or another regular browser while the client handles the Reticulum connection.

Most of our users browse this way. It allows them to use familiar navigation and keep network pages alongside the other things they do in their browser.

Messaging & connections

The client also handles LXMF messaging, identities, contacts and network connections. These functions sit alongside browsing so users can work from the same application.

projects/groupchat:
ciXnet GroupChat hosts channels on Reticulum. Each channel has its own LXMF address. Members send messages to that address, and the host forwards them to the other members.

In development

ChannelsAdministrationCommands

Using a channel

A channel can be used from NomadNet, Sideband or another LXMF client. Once you are a member, send text to the channel’s LXMF address to take part. The sender receives no duplicate copy of their own post.

Channels can allow open joining or require approval. In ordinary chat mode, members can post. Announcement mode restricts posting to administrators and designated superusers.

SENDYour LXMF clientMessage the channel address
→
FORWARDGroupChat hostChecks channel membership
→
RECEIVEOther membersDelivered through LXMF

Membership & administration

The host provides management pages through NomadNet and NomadPL. Both use the same channel settings and database. Identified users can create up to five groups.

The owner can appoint administrators. Administrators manage requests, invite members, change posting rules and set the topic. Superusers can post in announcement channels without receiving administrative permissions.

Logs & inactive channels

New groups begin with private logs. Administrators can choose to make a channel’s saved log public. Private logs require membership or service moderation rights.

After seven days without an accepted post, a channel stops announcing periodically. Members can reactivate it through the management pages or by posting to its known address.

Common commands

Send commands directly to the channel’s LXMF address.

CommandAction
/helpShow available commands
/joinJoin or request membership
/leaveLeave the channel
/membersShow the member list
/topicRead the channel topic
/reactivateResume channel announcements

Hosting & configuration

The host implementation is under development. Public source and setup links will be added here when the project is published. The ciXnet public service has not launched.
field-notes/vehicle-nodes: Leaving the node in the vehicle

A small node already connected and powered is easier to use than equipment that has to be unpacked before every trip.

Ready when people need it

Small LoRa nodes with Bluetooth let phones and laptops connect to the network. We began leaving more of these nodes permanently installed, including wiring them into vehicles.

That removes several steps from each use. There is no separate device to find, charge and remember to bring. The node is already there, and the user connects from their phone or laptop.

More access points

We now take a more-is-more approach to these inexpensive nodes. Putting them where people spend time makes access more convenient. As people had less equipment to handle, they used the network more often.

LoRa continues to serve these last-mile connections. Traffic between our network nodes is carried over HaLow links.

Hardware overview →Backbone links →
field-notes/halow-backbone:
Getting people to use the network regularly changed what we needed from the connections between nodes.

When airtime filled up

LoRa was inexpensive and gave us useful reach. Once a few people were active at the same time, however, the available airtime filled surprisingly quickly. Traffic backed up and the backbone connections became choppy.

We had been working to make the network comfortable enough for daily use. That meant the links between nodes needed to carry the combined activity of several users.

The change to HaLow

Moving those links to Wi-Fi HaLow removed the bottleneck we had been experiencing. In our installations, it gave us comparable range, with some links reaching farther than our previous LoRa connections.

We still use LoRa where its cost and reach make it useful for the last mile. HaLow carries traffic between nodes.

A node assembly

The illustrated assembly puts a Raspberry Pi, battery, charge controller and radios inside an inexpensive cooler. The HaLow bridge connects to the Pi through Ethernet. A USB connection joins the LoRa node to the Pi.

This arrangement brings the backbone and local radio access together at the same node.

projects/connect:
Connect is the gateway component of ciXnet: a way into the network and a place for LXMF messages to wait for recipients who are offline.

Connecting to the network

A gateway accepts Reticulum connections and carries traffic to other reachable destinations. It provides an entry point for clients connecting over an existing IP link.

Our host software combines inbound Reticulum TCP connectivity, LXMF propagation and hosted information pages. The service identities and destinations are separate, even when they run on the same computer.

Messages for offline recipients

LXMF propagation stores encrypted messages for later retrieval. A connected client can retrieve messages addressed to it when it returns. This is part of how we make messaging useful when people are not online at the same time.

Connection settings

The public gateway endpoint and propagation address have not been announced. They will be listed here when the service is ready for outside connections.

network/reticulum:
Reticulum is networking software for connecting applications across radio links, local networks and internet connections. It provides addressing, encrypted communication and routing between connected systems.

Different links in one network

A Reticulum network can combine several kinds of connection. A radio link can join a network carried over Ethernet or Wi-Fi, with transport nodes forwarding traffic between them.

Local communication can operate without internet access when a path exists between the devices. An internet connection can also carry Reticulum traffic between distant locations.

Applications & addresses

Applications use destination addresses derived from cryptographic identities. Reticulum handles communication with those destinations; applications provide functions such as messaging and publishing pages.

ApplicationsMessaging, pages and services
↔
ReticulumAddresses, encryption and routing
↔
ConnectionsRadio, Ethernet and IP links

How ciXnet uses it

Reticulum is the networking layer behind ciXnet. We use HaLow for backbone connections and LoRa nodes for local access. Our client provides messaging, a built-in browser and a bridge for browsing through Chrome or another regular browser.

NomadPL carries pages and applications over Reticulum. retdns resolves names to destination addresses. These are separate projects built on the same networking layer.

field-notes/opening-up-to-the-community:
18 November 2026

Over the past few years, we have been building a network and developing the software we needed to use it. Much of that work happened within our own group, with changes driven by the people using the network and the problems we encountered along the way.

In November, we decided to start publishing those tools and programs on GitHub.

Our work covers several parts of the network: client software, publishing, name resolution, messaging and the libraries behind them. These projects grew together, often because something we wanted to do was difficult or missing. Making the network easier to use became a large part of that work. We wanted people to use it regularly, through interfaces they were comfortable with, without needing to understand everything happening underneath.

Publishing the code gives other people a chance to try those approaches, examine how they work and build on them. It also gives us a chance to hear from people using different hardware, different configurations and networks with requirements beyond our own.

The rollout will happen gradually and will continue through March 2027. During that time, we will be preparing and publishing the remaining projects, libraries, documentation and configuration examples. Until that process is complete, the public repositories may lag behind the versions running on our own network. Afterward, we will aim to keep ongoing development in step with the public repositories.

We would like to hear from anyone trying the ciXnet client, running one of our programs or using our libraries in their own software. If something is confusing, behaves unexpectedly or makes an ordinary task harder than it should be, that is useful feedback. Reports about installation and first use are particularly welcome: familiarity can make it easy for us to overlook steps that someone new has no reason to know.

We are also interested in what people build with the libraries. If you use them in another application, adapt a tool for your own network or find an approach we have not considered, please share it. Questions about how the code fits together can help us identify where documentation needs more attention.

Alongside the software, we will publish accounts of how we use the equipment and what we have learned from running the network.

Please use the relevant project’s GitHub Issues for feedback, support questions and bug reports. For problems, include the version you are using, your operating system and enough detail for us to reproduce what happened. Suggestions and contributions are welcome there too.

You can find the projects and their repositories through the ciXnet project pages, or browse the code on GitHub.
